title: Client-IP trust model is not fail-safe: with the shipped trusted-proxy-hops=0 the admin IP allowlist and the anonymous per-IP rate limit are bypassable via a spoofed X-Forwarded-For, and the WebFlux tests override the two decisive properties
actual: gateway-service/application.yml line 4 sets server.forward-headers-strategy: framework. In Spring Boot 4.1.1, ReactiveWebServerConfiguration.forwardedHeaderTransformer() is registered with @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "server.forward-headers-strategy", havingValue = "framework"), so the ForwardedHeaderTransformer IS active in this WebFlux gateway; it rewrites the request remote address from the client-supplied X-Forwarded-For, taking the LEFTMOST entry. ClientIpResolver and RateLimitKeyResolver only use XForwardedRemoteAddressResolver when trustedProxyHops > 0; with the shipped default of 0 they fall back to exchange.getRequest().getRemoteAddress(), which is now the attacker-controlled header value. WebFluxIpAllowlistTests overrides BOTH decisive properties (server.forward-headers-strategy=NONE and gateway.rate-limit.trusted-proxy-hops=1) so the suite never exercises the shipped configuration. docker-compose.prod.yml defaults hops to 1; docker-compose.yml and .env.example use 0.
expected: The client IP used for the admin allowlist and for the anonymous rate-limit bucket must come from the trusted end of the X-Forwarded-For chain, and the shipped default must be the safe one. The test suite must exercise the production configuration.
trigger: Any deployment that runs with trusted-proxy-hops=0 (the shipped .env.example value and the docker-compose.yml default) and receives a request with an attacker-chosen X-Forwarded-For header.
root_cause: The 'prevent forwarded IP spoofing' fix (commit 90cea14, H28) is only effective when trusted-proxy-hops >= 1. The code and the tests both assume that value, but the shipped default is 0, and no startup validation ties the two settings together.
consequences: With hops=0, an unauthenticated caller sets X-Forwarded-For: <an address inside the allowlist CIDR> and the admin IP allowlist grants access. The same header defeats the anonymous 100 rps / 200 burst per-IP bucket, because each request lands in a fresh ip:<spoofed> bucket. When the gateway sits directly behind a load balancer with hops=0, the opposite failure also occurs: every anonymous client shares the proxy's single bucket, so one client can exhaust the limit for all of them.
remediation: Make the safe posture the default and validate it at startup: set server.forward-headers-strategy to NONE in the gateway so the gateway resolves the client IP itself, set the default trusted-proxy-hops to 1, and fail startup when the strategy is 'framework' while trusted-proxy-hops is 0. Remove the property overrides from WebFluxIpAllowlistTests so the suite runs against the production configuration, and add a regression test asserting that a spoofed leftmost X-Forwarded-For does not grant allowlist access.
regression_test: WebFlux integration test with the production properties: a request with X-Forwarded-For set to an allowlisted address must still be rejected; a request with hops=0 configuration must fail the application startup.

title: The gateway performs no JWT audience validation - a token minted for any client in the realm is accepted at the edge
actual: The gateway depends only on common-core, not common-security, so common-security's BaseSecurityConfig (issuer + timestamp + audience validator chain) never applies - SecurityAutoConfiguration is @ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = SERVLET) and the gateway is reactive. SecurityConfig builds a ServerHttpSecurity chain with oauth2ResourceServer(jwt(Customizer.withDefaults())) and the only JWT configuration is spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri. Spring Boot's reactive auto-configuration therefore builds a NimbusReactiveJwtDecoder whose validator is JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer(...) - issuer and timestamp only. There is no JwtDecoder bean, no audience validator and no JwtRolesConverter in the gateway source.
expected: The edge must reject a token whose audience does not include the client the gateway serves, and it must map Keycloak realm roles into authorities so route-level role rules can be expressed.
trigger: Any valid realm token, including one issued for a low-privilege or unrelated client, presented to the gateway.
root_cause: The audience validator added to common-security (the 'C1 fix') is implemented in a servlet-only auto-configuration, so the reactive edge - the one place where the check matters most - has no equivalent.
consequences: Horizontal privilege escalation at the edge: a token issued to a different client is honoured by the gateway, and the gateway's public-endpoint list is the only remaining boundary. Roles are not mapped to authorities either, so any future hasRole() route rule in the gateway would behave unexpectedly.
remediation: Add a reactive JWT decoder to the gateway that applies the same validator chain as common-security (issuer, timestamp, and audience when configured), and map realm_access.roles to authorities. Extract the validator chain into common-security so both stacks share one implementation.
regression_test: WebFlux integration test: a token with aud=[other-client] must be rejected with 401 by the gateway.

title: Gateway CORS combines allowCredentials=true with the shipped wildcard origin pattern, enabling cross-origin credentialed data theft
actual: SecurityConfig.corsWebFilter() sets config.setAllowCredentials(true) and config.setAllowedOriginPatterns(properties.corsAllowedOriginPatterns()). The application.yml requires the property with the placeholder ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS:?...}, but .env.example line 157 ships CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS=*. With allowedOriginPatterns containing '*' and allowCredentials=true, Spring echoes the request Origin instead of sending '*' and adds Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, so any website can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the gateway and read the responses. The fail-fast placeholder only covers the case where the variable is absent; the shipped example supplies the wildcard value, so it never triggers.
expected: allowCredentials=true must only ever be combined with an explicit origin allow-list. A wildcard origin must not be shippable with credentials enabled.
trigger: A deployment that copies .env.example (the shipped default) into the environment.
root_cause: The configuration guard validates presence, not value; the credentialed-CORS hazard is a property of the combination, not of the variable alone.
consequences: Any web page can read authenticated responses from the gateway on behalf of a logged-in user - classic cross-origin data theft. The gateway is the only component that sets allowCredentials(true); the shared servlet stack defaults it to false.
remediation: Validate the combination at startup: refuse to boot when allowCredentials is true and the resolved origin patterns contain '*'. Ship an explicit localhost allow-list in .env.example instead of '*'.
regression_test: Configuration test: starting the gateway with CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS='*' must fail with a clear error.

title: The edge rate limiter uses in-process bucket4j buckets, so the effective limit scales with the replica count
actual: RateLimitFilter's javadoc states 'Buckets live in-process (single gateway instance, V1)'. The buckets are a Caffeine cache of Bucket4j buckets keyed by scope + client IP, held in each gateway JVM. The two Redis-backed tiers (global 2000/4000 and per-client 100/200) are distributed; this third tier is not.
expected: A documented, consistent rate-limit model. If the edge scopes are intended to be fleet-wide, they need the same Redis-backed implementation as the other two tiers.
trigger: Running more than one gateway replica.
root_cause: The tier was implemented as an in-process optimisation and labelled 'V1' without a migration plan or an operational note that the limit is per replica.
consequences: The backoffice (10 rpm) and search (60 rpm) limits are multiplied by the replica count: with 4 replicas a single client can make 40 backoffice requests per minute. This weakens exactly the control that protects the backoffice.
remediation: Move the edge buckets to the same Redis-backed RedisRateLimiter used by the other tiers, or document the per-replica semantics explicitly in the deployment runbook and align the configured values with the replica count.
regression_test: Multi-instance test: two gateway replicas must share the edge limit bucket.

title: The backoffice admin IP allowlist is INACTIVE by default in every shipped configuration
actual: AdminIpAllowlistFilter.filter() returns chain.filter(exchange) immediately when properties.active() is false. docker-compose.prod.yml ships ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST: ${ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST:-} - an empty value, which is INACTIVE. .env.prod.example does not define ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST. The inline comment acknowledges that 'env ABSENT or EMPTY STRING = filter INACTIVE (allow-all)'.
expected: A network-layer control in front of the backoffice should fail closed in production, or its absence should block startup.
trigger: A production deployment that does not explicitly populate ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST.
root_cause: The control is opt-in with an allow-all default, and the default is what the production compose file ships.
consequences: The backoffice (products, categories, brands, promotions, tax, notifications, payments, ratings, shipments, search) is reachable from any network origin; only the JWT role check stands between an attacker and administrative functions. The compose comment documents the hazard but nothing enforces it.
remediation: Make the allowlist mandatory in the prod profile (fail startup when absent or empty) or add a startup guard that logs a prominent warning and exposes a health indicator so the gap is visible in monitoring.
regression_test: Configuration test: the prod profile must fail to start without ADMIN_IP_ALLOWLIST.

title: .env.prod.example omits CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS, which the gateway requires to start
actual: The gateway resolves gateway.cors-allowed-origin-patterns from ${CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS:?CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS must be set explicitly}. docker-compose.yml supplies it with a required placeholder, and docker-compose.prod.yml inherits that mapping, but .env.prod.example never defines the variable.
expected: Every variable the production stack requires is present in the production environment template.
root_cause: The template and the required-placeholder set drifted apart.
consequences: The gateway container fails to start with an unresolved-placeholder error - a fail-fast behaviour, but one that surfaces as an outage during deployment rather than as a configuration review finding.
remediation: Add CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGIN_PATTERNS (and any other required variable) to .env.prod.example with an explicit non-wildcard value.
regression_test: CI check: render the prod compose configuration and assert every required placeholder resolves.
